claim: Rod-shaped mycobacteria expand from their poles.
source: Rod-shaped mycobacteria expand from their poles, yet d-amino acid probes label cell wall peptidoglycan in this genus at both the poles and sidewall.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations in the abstract and is consistent with established literature on mycobacterial growth.

claim: d-amino acid probes label cell wall peptidoglycan in mycobacteria at both the poles and sidewall.
source: Rod-shaped mycobacteria expand from their poles, yet d-amino acid probes label cell wall peptidoglycan in this genus at both the poles and sidewall.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Monopeptide incorporation was decreased by antibiotics that block peptidoglycan synthesis.
source: Monopeptide incorporation was decreased by antibiotics that block peptidoglycan synthesis or l,d-transpeptidation and in an l,d-transpeptidase mutant.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B where antibiotics affecting peptidoglycan synthesis reduce monopeptide probe incorporation.

claim: Monopeptide incorporation was decreased by antibiotics that block l,d-transpeptidation.
source: Monopeptide incorporation was decreased by antibiotics that block peptidoglycan synthesis or l,d-transpeptidation and in an l,d-transpeptidase mutant.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3B showing that imipenem, which inhibits l,d-transpeptidases, reduces monopeptide labeling.

claim: Monopeptide incorporation was decreased in an l,d-transpeptidase mutant.
source: Monopeptide incorporation was decreased by antibiotics that block peptidoglycan synthesis or l,d-transpeptidation and in an l,d-transpeptidase mutant.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3F showing reduced labeling in ΔldtABE mutants.

claim: Dipeptides complemented defects in d-alanine synthesis.
source: Dipeptides complemented defects in d-alanine synthesis or ligation and were present in lipid-linked peptidoglycan precursors.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4A showing that alkDADA rescues growth of Δalr mutant.

claim: Dipeptides complemented defects in d-alanine ligation.
source: Dipeptides complemented defects in d-alanine synthesis or ligation and were present in lipid-linked peptidoglycan precursors.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4B showing that alkDADA rescues growth of ddlAts mutant.

claim: Dipeptides were present in lipid-linked peptidoglycan precursors.
source: Dipeptides complemented defects in d-alanine synthesis or ligation and were present in lipid-linked peptidoglycan precursors.
evidence: This is supported by biochemical data in Figure 5B and 5C showing detection of alkDADA and azDADA in lipid-linked precursors.

claim: Monopeptide-marked l,d-transpeptidase remodeling was coincident with mycomembrane metabolism at the poles.
source: Characterizing probe uptake pathways allowed us to localize peptidoglycan metabolism with precision: monopeptide-marked l,d-transpeptidase remodeling and dipeptide-marked synthesis were coincident with mycomembrane metabolism at the poles, septum and sidewall.
evidence: This is supported by colocalization data in Figure 2B and 2C showing similar distributions of RADA and OalkTMM at poles.

claim: Monopeptide-marked l,d-transpeptidase remodeling was coincident with mycomembrane metabolism at the septum.
source: Characterizing probe uptake pathways allowed us to localize peptidoglycan metabolism with precision: monopeptide-marked l,d-transpeptidase remodeling and dipeptide-marked synthesis were coincident with mycomembrane metabolism at the poles, septum and sidewall.
evidence: This is supported by colocalization data in Figure 2C showing similar distributions at septa.

claim: Monopeptide-marked l,d-transpeptidase remodeling was coincident with mycomembrane metabolism at the sidewall.
source: Characterizing probe uptake pathways allowed us to localize peptidoglycan metabolism with precision: monopeptide-marked l,d-transpeptidase remodeling and dipeptide-marked synthesis were coincident with mycomembrane metabolism at the poles, septum and sidewall.
evidence: This is supported by colocalization data in Figure 2B and 2C showing similar distributions along the sidewall.

claim: Dipeptide-marked synthesis was coincident with mycomembrane metabolism at the poles.
source: Characterizing probe uptake pathways allowed us to localize peptidoglycan metabolism with precision: monopeptide-marked l,d-transpeptidase remodeling and dipeptide-marked synthesis were coincident with mycomembrane metabolism at the poles, septum and sidewall.
evidence: This is supported by colocalization data in Figure 2B and 2C showing similar distributions of alkDADA and OalkTMM at poles.

claim: Dipeptide-marked synthesis was coincident with mycomembrane metabolism at the septum.
source: Characterizing probe uptake pathways allowed us to localize peptidoglycan metabolism with precision: monopeptide-marked l,d-transpeptidase remodeling and dipeptide-marked synthesis were coincident with mycomembrane metabolism at the poles, septum and sidewall.
evidence: This is supported by colocalization data in Figure 2C showing similar distributions at septa.

claim: Dipeptide-marked synthesis was coincident with mycomembrane metabolism at the sidewall.
source: Characterizing probe uptake pathways allowed us to localize peptidoglycan metabolism with precision: monopeptide-marked l,d-transpeptidase remodeling and dipeptide-marked synthesis were coincident with mycomembrane metabolism at the poles, septum and sidewall.
evidence: This is supported by colocalization data in Figure 2B and 2C showing similar distributions along the sidewall.

claim: Fluorescent penicillin-marked d,d-transpeptidation occurs around the cell perimeter.
source: Fluorescent pencillin-marked d,d-transpeptidation around the cell perimeter further suggested that the mycobacterial sidewall is a site of cell wall assembly.
evidence: This is supported by Bocillin labeling data in Figure 5—figure supplement 3B and 3C showing fluorescence around the cell perimeter.

claim: The mycobacterial sidewall is a site of cell wall assembly.
source: Fluorescent pencillin-marked d,d-transpeptidation around the cell perimeter further suggested that the mycobacterial sidewall is a site of cell wall assembly.
evidence: This is inferred from multiple lines of evidence including Bocillin labeling, PonA1 localization, and dipeptide probe incorporation at the sidewall.

claim: Polar peptidoglycan synthesis was associated with cell elongation.
source: While polar peptidoglycan synthesis was associated with cell elongation, sidewall synthesis responded to cell wall damage.
evidence: This is supported by pulse-chase data in Figure 5—figure supplement 4 showing fluorescence dilution at poles during growth.

claim: Sidewall synthesis responded to cell wall damage.
source: While polar peptidoglycan synthesis was associated with cell elongation, sidewall synthesis responded to cell wall damage.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 6B showing increased sidewall labeling after muramidase treatment.

claim: Peptidoglycan editing along the sidewall may support cell wall robustness in pole-growing mycobacteria.
source: Peptidoglycan editing along the sidewall may support cell wall robustness in pole-growing mycobacteria.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observation that sidewall synthesis increases upon damage.

claim: Model, rod-shaped organisms such as Escherichia coli and Bacillus subtilis elongate across a broad swath of the cell.
source: Model, rod-shaped organisms such as Escherichia coli and Bacillus subtilis elongate across a broad swath of the cell (de Pedro et al., 1997; Daniel and Errington, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature on bacterial cell growth.

claim: Mycobacterial cells extend from narrower polar regions.
source: Mycobacterial cells, by contrast, extend from narrower polar regions (Aldridge et al., 2012; Santi et al., 2013; Meniche et al., 2014; Thanky et al., 2007; Kieser and Rubin, 2014; Singh et al., 2013; Joyce et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature on mycobacterial growth.

claim: If polar growth and division are the only sites of cell wall synthesis in mycobacteria, the entire lateral surface of the cell must be inert.
source: For example, if polar growth and division are the only sites of cell wall synthesis in mycobacteria, the entire lateral surface of the cell must be inert (Aldridge et al., 2012; Brown et al., 2012; Kuru et al., 2012; Zupan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the assumption of polar-only growth, supported by citations.

claim: An expanse of non-renewable surface could leave the cell vulnerable to environmental or immune insults.
source: Such an expanse of non-renewable surface could leave the cell vulnerable to environmental or immune insults.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential consequences of having an inert lateral surface.

claim: d-amino acid probes have been shown to incorporate into peptidoglycan in other species.
source: Intriguingly, d-amino acid probes, which in other species have been shown to incorporate into peptidoglycan (de Pedro et al., 1997; Kuru et al., 2012; Siegrist et al., 2013), label both the poles and sidewall of mycobacteria (Meniche et al., 2014; Siegrist et al., 2013; Boutte et al., 2016; Botella et al., 2017; Schubert et al., 2017; Rodriguez-Rivera et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature on d-amino acid probe incorporation.

claim: d-amino acid probes label both the poles and sidewall of mycobacteria.
source: Intriguingly, d-amino acid probes, which in other species have been shown to incorporate into peptidoglycan (de Pedro et al., 1997; Kuru et al., 2012; Siegrist et al., 2013), label both the poles and sidewall of mycobacteria (Meniche et al., 2014; Siegrist et al., 2013; Boutte et al., 2016; Botella et al., 2017; Schubert et al., 2017; Rodriguez-Rivera et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations and is a key observation that motivated the study.

claim: Peptidoglycan synthetic enzymes have been detected at the mycobacterial cell tips.
source: The localization of these molecules is supported by the detection of peptidoglycan synthetic enzymes at the mycobacterial cell tips and periphery (Meniche et al., 2014; Joyce et al., 2012; Hett et al., 2010; Kieser et al., 2015a; Plocinski et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature on enzyme localization.

claim: Peptidoglycan synthetic enzymes have been detected at the mycobacterial cell periphery.
source: The localization of these molecules is supported by the detection of peptidoglycan synthetic enzymes at the mycobacterial cell tips and periphery (Meniche et al., 2014; Joyce et al., 2012; Hett et al., 2010; Kieser et al., 2015a; Plocinski et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature on enzyme localization.

claim: Both intracellular and extracellular incorporation pathways have been characterized or hypothesized for d-amino acid probes.
source: However, both intracellular and extracellular incorporation pathways have been characterized or hypothesized for d-amino acid probes, complicating the interpretation of labeling patterns (Siegrist et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article on probe incorporation pathways.

claim: Intracellular uptake implies that the probe enters the biosynthetic pathway at an early stage and therefore marks nascent cell wall.
source: Intracellular uptake implies that the probe enters the biosynthetic pathway at an early stage, and therefore marks nascent cell wall.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the implications of intracellular probe incorporation.

claim: Extracellular incorporation suggests that the probe enters the pathway at a later stage and/or is part of enzymatic remodeling.
source: Extracellular incorporation, on the other hand, suggests that the probe enters the pathway at a later stage and/or is part of enzymatic remodeling of the macromolecule in question.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the implications of extracellular probe incorporation.

claim: The extent to which peptidoglycan synthesis and remodeling are linked is not clear.
source: The extent to which peptidoglycan synthesis and remodeling are linked is not clear (Brown et al., 2012; de Pedro and Cava, 2015; Glauner and Höltje, 1990) and may vary with species and external milieu.
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature discussing the relationship between synthesis and remodeling.

claim: The relationship between peptidoglycan synthesis and remodeling may vary with species and external milieu.
source: The extent to which peptidoglycan synthesis and remodeling are linked is not clear (Brown et al., 2012; de Pedro and Cava, 2015; Glauner and Höltje, 1990) and may vary with species and external milieu.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on general biological knowledge.

claim: In Mycobacterium tuberculosis, there is indirect but abundant data that suggest substantial cell envelope remodeling during infection when growth and peptidoglycan synthesis are presumed to be slow or nonexistent.
source: In Mycobacterium tuberculosis, for example, there is indirect but abundant data that suggest that there is a substantial cell envelope remodeling during infection when growth and peptidoglycan synthesis are presumed to be slow or nonexistent (Kieser and Rubin, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to literature on M. tuberculosis cell envelope dynamics during infection.

claim: At least two pieces of evidence suggest that d-alanine-d-alanine dipeptide probes are incorporated into peptidoglycan via the cytoplasmic MurF ligase.
source: At least two pieces of evidence suggest that d-alanine-d-alanine dipeptide probes are incorporated into peptidoglycan via the cytoplasmic MurF ligase (Liechti et al., 2014; Sarkar et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to two studies providing evidence for MurF-dependent incorporation.

claim: Derivatives of d-alanine-d-alanine rescue the growth of Chlamydia trachomatis treated with d-cycloserine.
source: First, derivatives of d-alanine-d-alanine rescue the growth of Chlamydia trachomatis treated with d-cycloserine, an antibiotic that inhibits peptidoglycan synthesis by inhibiting the production and self-ligation of d-alanine in the cytoplasm (Liechti et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on C. trachomatis.

claim: d-cycloserine inhibits peptidoglycan synthesis by inhibiting the production and self-ligation of d-alanine in the cytoplasm.
source: First, derivatives of d-alanine-d-alanine rescue the growth of Chlamydia trachomatis treated with d-cycloserine, an antibiotic that inhibits peptidoglycan synthesis by inhibiting the production and self-ligation of d-alanine in the cytoplasm (Liechti et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of d-cycloserine, supported by citation.

claim: B. subtilis cells stripped of mature peptidoglycan by lysozyme treatment retain a small amount of dipeptide-derived fluorescence.
source: Second, B. subtilis cells stripped of mature peptidoglycan by lysozyme treatment retain a small amount of dipeptide-derived fluorescence (Sarkar et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on B. subtilis.

claim: Formal demonstration of intracellular incorporation requires direct evidence that the probe labels peptidoglycan precursors.
source: While these data are suggestive, formal demonstration of intracellular incorporation requires direct evidence that the probe labels peptidoglycan precursors.
evidence: This is a statement about the standards of evidence needed to demonstrate intracellular incorporation.

claim: Better characterization of the metabolic fate of probes would increase the precision of conclusions that can be drawn from labeling experiments.
source: More broadly, better characterization of the metabolic fate of probes would increase the precision of conclusions that can be drawn from labeling experiments (Boyce et al., 2011; Qin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a general statement about the importance of understanding probe metabolism, supported by citations.

claim: Monopeptide d-amino acid probes chiefly reported peptidoglycan remodeling by l,d-transpeptidases.
source: Monopeptide d-amino acid probes chiefly reported peptidoglycan remodeling by l,d-transpeptidases while dipeptides marked lipid-linked peptidoglycan precursors.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by antibiotic sensitivity and mutant analysis data.

claim: Dipeptides marked lipid-linked peptidoglycan precursors.
source: Monopeptide d-amino acid probes chiefly reported peptidoglycan remodeling by l,d-transpeptidases while dipeptides marked lipid-linked peptidoglycan precursors.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by biochemical detection of labeled precursors.

claim: All the probes tested labeled the poles and sidewall of mycobacteria.
source: All the probes tested labeled the poles and sidewall of mycobacteria, indicating that cell wall metabolism in these regions comprises both synthetic and remodeling reactions.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data in Figure 2A showing labeling at both locations.

claim: Cell wall metabolism at the poles and sidewall comprises both synthetic and remodeling reactions.
source: All the probes tested labeled the poles and sidewall of mycobacteria, indicating that cell wall metabolism in these regions comprises both synthetic and remodeling reactions.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both synthesis-marking and remodeling-marking probes label these regions.

claim: Peptidoglycan assembly along the mycobacterial periphery did not support obvious surface expansion.
source: While peptidoglycan assembly along the mycobacterial periphery did not support obvious surface expansion, it was greatly enhanced by cell wall damage.
evidence: This is supported by pulse-chase data in Figure 5—figure supplement 4 showing no detectable sidewall expansion.

claim: Peptidoglycan assembly along the mycobacterial periphery was greatly enhanced by cell wall damage.
source: While peptidoglycan assembly along the mycobacterial periphery did not support obvious surface expansion, it was greatly enhanced by cell wall damage.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 6B showing increased sidewall labeling after muramidase treatment.

claim: Insertion of peptidoglycan building blocks directly along the cell periphery would enable a real-time, comprehensive response to damage.
source: More specifically, we reasoned that insertion of peptidoglycan building blocks directly along the cell periphery would enable a real-time, comprehensive response to damage (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the function of sidewall peptidoglycan synthesis.

claim: M. smegmatis was incubated for ~10% generation in probe.
source: After M. smegmatis cells were incubated for ~10% generation in probe, high-resolution and quantitative microscopy revealed that they had asymmetric, bidirectional gradients of fluorescence that emanated from the poles and continued along the sidewall (Figure 2A).
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions used in the study.

claim: M. smegmatis cells had asymmetric, bidirectional gradients of fluorescence that emanated from the poles and continued along the sidewall.
source: After M. smegmatis cells were incubated for ~10% generation in probe, high-resolution and quantitative microscopy revealed that they had asymmetric, bidirectional gradients of fluorescence that emanated from the poles and continued along the sidewall (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from microscopy data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Polar gradients of dipeptide labeling were apparent in live cells when azDADA incorporation was detected by CuAAC.
source: Polar gradients of dipeptide labeling were also apparent in live cells when we detected azido-d-alanine-d-alanine (azDADA or ADA-DA, [Liechti et al., 2014]) incorporation by either CuAAC (using low copper, bio-friendly reaction conditions ([Yang et al., 2014], Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) or by copper-free, strain-promoted azide-alkyne cycloaddition (SPAAC, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Polar gradients of dipeptide labeling were apparent in live cells when azDADA incorporation was detected by SPAAC.
source: Polar gradients of dipeptide labeling were also apparent in live cells when we detected azido-d-alanine-d-alanine (azDADA or ADA-DA, [Liechti et al., 2014]) incorporation by either CuAAC (using low copper, bio-friendly reaction conditions ([Yang et al., 2014], Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) or by copper-free, strain-promoted azide-alkyne cycloaddition (SPAAC, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The mycobacterial cell envelope is comprised of covalently bound peptidoglycan, arabinogalactan and mycolic acids, as well as intercalated glycolipids and a thick capsule.
source: The mycobacterial cell envelope is comprised of covalently bound peptidoglycan, arabinogalactan and mycolic acids, as well as intercalated glycolipids and a thick capsule ([Puffal et al., 2018], Figure 1B).
evidence: This is established knowledge about mycobacterial cell envelope structure, supported by citation.

claim: Assembly of the envelope layers has long been presumed to be spatially coincident.
source: Assembly of the envelope layers has long been presumed to be spatially coincident.
evidence: This is a statement about a prevailing assumption in the field.

claim: Ligation of arabinogalactan to peptidoglycan occurs concurrently with crosslinking of the latter by transpeptidases.
source: This is largely based on biochemical data suggesting that ligation of arabinogalactan to peptidoglycan occurs concurrently with crosslinking of the latter by transpeptidases (Hancock et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to biochemical studies.

claim: Cytoplasmic enzymes that mediate arabinogalactan and mycomembrane synthesis are enriched at the poles.
source: We and others have found that cytoplasmic enzymes that mediate arabinogalactan and mycomembrane synthesis are enriched at the poles but also present along the periphery of the cell (Meniche et al., 2014; Hayashi et al., 2016; Carel et al., 2014), as is metabolic labeling by OalkTMM and NalkTMM ([Backus et al., 2011; Swarts et al., 2012; Foley et al., 2016], Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published localization studies.

claim: Cytoplasmic enzymes that mediate arabinogalactan and mycomembrane synthesis are present along the periphery of the cell.
source: We and others have found that cytoplasmic enzymes that mediate arabinogalactan and mycomembrane synthesis are enriched at the poles but also present along the periphery of the cell (Meniche et al., 2014; Hayashi et al., 2016; Carel et al., 2014), as is metabolic labeling by OalkTMM and NalkTMM ([Backus et al., 2011; Swarts et al., 2012; Foley et al., 2016], Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published localization studies.

claim: OalkTMM and NalkTMM predominantly mark covalent mycolates and trehalose dimycolate, respectively, in the mycomembrane.
source: OalkTMM and NalkTMM are trehalose monomycolate derivatives that predominantly mark covalent mycolates and trehalose dimycolate, respectively, in the mycomembrane (Figure 1B, [Foley et al., 2016]).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study characterizing these probes.

claim: The cell pole with brighter RADA fluorescence also had more alkDADA labeling.
source: The cell pole with brighter RADA fluorescence also had more alkDADA or OalkTMM labeling (Figure 2B), suggesting that the polar orientation of peptidoglycan and mycomembrane metabolism is coincident.
evidence: This is a direct observation from dual-labeling microscopy data in Figure 2B.

claim: The cell pole with brighter RADA fluorescence also had more OalkTMM labeling.
source: The cell pole with brighter RADA fluorescence also had more alkDADA or OalkTMM labeling (Figure 2B), suggesting that the polar orientation of peptidoglycan and mycomembrane metabolism is coincident.
evidence: This is a direct observation from dual-labeling microscopy data in Figure 2B.

claim: The polar orientation of peptidoglycan and mycomembrane metabolism is coincident.
source: The cell pole with brighter RADA fluorescence also had more alkDADA or OalkTMM labeling (Figure 2B), suggesting that the polar orientation of peptidoglycan and mycomembrane metabolism is coincident.
evidence: This is inferred from the colocalization of different probes at the same pole.

claim: RADA, alkDADA and OalkTMM have similar, average distributions at the poles and peripheries of the cells.
source: We then compared the fluorescence intensity profiles of cells that had been individually labeled with the probes, and found similar, average distributions of RADA, alkDADA and OalkTMM at the poles and peripheries of the cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of fluorescence profiles shown in Figure 2C.

claim: alkDA incorporates into the cell surface of M. tuberculosis.
source: We previously showed that alkDA incorporates into the cell surface of the organism (Siegrist et al., 2013) but were unable to stain the entire population of bacteria.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: HADA and NADA incubation yielded well-defined fluorescent populations in M. tuberculosis.
source: HADA and NADA incubation yielded well-defined fluorescent populations (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: RADA labeled the entire M. tuberculosis population, albeit with greater cell-to-cell variability in fluorescence intensity.
source: RADA also labeled the entire M. tuberculosis population, albeit with greater cell-to-cell variability in fluorescence intensity.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Approximately 5 to 10% of M. tuberculosis cells that had been incubated in alkDA, alkDADA or OalkTMM showed azido-coumarin fluorescence under optimized CuAAC conditions.
source: Under our optimized conditions we detected azido-coumarin fluorescence from ~5 to 10% of cells that had been incubated in alkDA, alkDADA or OalkTMM (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry and microscopy data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B and C.

claim: HADA, alkDADA and OalkTMM tagging in M. tuberculosis produced cells that had a mixture of sidewall and polar fluorescence.
source: HADA, alkDADA and OalkTMM tagging all produced cells that had a mixture of sidewall and polar fluorescence (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C) but exhibited a higher degree of cell-to-cell variability compared to M. smegmatis.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: M. tuberculosis exhibited a higher degree of cell-to-cell variability in labeling compared to M. smegmatis.
source: HADA, alkDADA and OalkTMM tagging all produced cells that had a mixture of sidewall and polar fluorescence (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C) but exhibited a higher degree of cell-to-cell variability compared to M. smegmatis.
evidence: This is a comparative observation based on microscopy data.

claim: Approximately 70–75% of HADA labeling in M. tuberculosis localized to the sidewall.
source: Approximately 70–75% of HADA labeling in M. tuberculosis localized to the sidewall compared to 63–64% for M. smegmatis (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis in Figure 2D.

claim: Approximately 63–64% of HADA labeling in M. smegmatis localized to the sidewall.
source: Approximately 70–75% of HADA labeling in M. tuberculosis localized to the sidewall compared to 63–64% for M. smegmatis (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis in Figure 2D.

claim: A greater proportion of peptidoglycan metabolism in M. tuberculosis likely occurs along the cell periphery than in M. smegmatis.
source: Thus, a greater proportion of peptidoglycan metabolism in M. tuberculosis likely occurs along the cell periphery than in M. smegmatis, although we cannot rule out a differential contribution of cyan autofluorescence in the two species (Patiño et al., 2008).
evidence: This is inferred from the quantitative comparison of sidewall labeling between the two species.

claim: OalkTMM and NalkTMM are inserted directly by the extracellular Antigen 85 complex into the mycomembrane.
source: OalkTMM and NalkTMM are inserted directly by the extracellular Antigen 85 complex into the mycomembrane (Foley et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study characterizing the incorporation mechanism of these probes.

claim: There are three potential pathways by which d-amino acid probes might incorporate into mycobacterial peptidoglycan: an intracellular, biosynthetic route and two extracellular routes, mediated by d,d-transpeptidase or l,d-transpeptidase remodeling enzymes.
source: However, there are three potential pathways by which d-amino acid probes might incorporate into mycobacterial peptidoglycan (Siegrist et al., 2015; Cava et al., 2011; Ngo et al., 2016): an intracellular, biosynthetic route and two extracellular routes, mediated by d,d-transpeptidase or l,d-transpeptidase remodeling enzymes (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about peptidoglycan metabolism pathways, supported by citations.

claim: Peptidoglycan remodeling, particularly by l,d-transpeptidases, may not strictly correlate with synthesis of the biopolymer.
source: Peptidoglycan remodeling, particularly by the l,d-transpeptidases abundantly encoded in the mycobacterial genome, may not strictly correlate with synthesis of the biopolymer (Brown et al., 2012; Kuru et al., 2012; de Pedro and Cava, 2015; Glauner and Höltje, 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on peptidoglycan remodeling.

claim: d-cycloserine is a cyclic analog of d-alanine that inhibits the d-alanine racemase (Alr) and ligase (DdlA) in mycobacteria.
source: d-cycloserine is a cyclic analog of d-alanine that inhibits the d-alanine racemase (Alr) and ligase (DdlA) in mycobacteria (Feng and Barletta, 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge about d-cycloserine mechanism, supported by citation.

claim: β-lactams like ampicillin together with the β-lactamase inhibitor clavulanate block d,d-transpeptidases and d,d-carboxypeptidases.
source: Together with the β-lactamase inhibitor clavulanate, β-lactams like ampicillin block d,d-transpeptidases and d,d-carboxypeptidases.
evidence: This is established knowledge about β-lactam antibiotic mechanisms.

claim: Carbapenems such as imipenem inhibit l,d-transpeptidases.
source: Broader spectrum carbapenems such as imipenem additionally inhibit l,d-transpeptidases (Kumar et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about carbapenem mechanisms, supported by citation.

claim: Vancomycin interferes with transpeptidation and transglycosylation by steric occlusion.
source: We also included vancomycin, an antibiotic that interferes with transpeptidation and transglycosylation by steric occlusion, to control for general defects in periplasmic peptidoglycan assembly.
evidence: This is established knowledge about vancomycin mechanism.

claim: Labeling for all single residue d-amino acid probes decreased significantly in response to imipenem treatment.
source: Within this time frame, labeling for all single residue d-amino acid probes decreased significantly in response to imipenem or d-cycloserine treatment (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3B.

claim: Labeling for all single residue d-amino acid probes decreased significantly in response to d-cycloserine treatment.
source: Within this time frame, labeling for all single residue d-amino acid probes decreased significantly in response to imipenem or d-cycloserine treatment (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3B.

claim: Labeling by the dipeptide probe was relatively resistant to imipenem and d-cycloserine.
source: By contrast, labeling by the dipeptide probe was relatively resistant to these antibiotics.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3B showing minimal effect of these antibiotics on alkDADA labeling.

claim: Neither vancomycin nor ampicillin had a clear effect on labeling by any of the probes.
source: Neither vancomycin nor ampicillin had a clear effect on labeling by any of the probes, indicating that cell death, disruption of peptidoglycan polymerization, and abrogration of d,d-transpeptidation do not explain the metabolic incorporation differences.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3B.

claim: Cell death, disruption of peptidoglycan polymerization, and abrogation of d,d-transpeptidation do not explain the metabolic incorporation differences.
source: Neither vancomycin nor ampicillin had a clear effect on labeling by any of the probes, indicating that cell death, disruption of peptidoglycan polymerization, and abrogration of d,d-transpeptidation do not explain the metabolic incorporation differences.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of effect of vancomycin and ampicillin on probe labeling.

claim: OalkTMM labeling was sensitive to d-cycloserine.
source: OalkTMM labeling was sensitive to d-cycloserine, but not to imipenem nor ampicillin, suggesting that transfer of mycolates to arabinogalactan may require peptidoglycan precursor synthesis but not transpeptidation.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3B.

claim: OalkTMM labeling was not sensitive to imipenem.
source: OalkTMM labeling was sensitive to d-cycloserine, but not to imipenem nor ampicillin, suggesting that transfer of mycolates to arabinogalactan may require peptidoglycan precursor synthesis but not transpeptidation.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3B.

claim: OalkTMM labeling was not sensitive to ampicillin.
source: OalkTMM labeling was sensitive to d-cycloserine, but not to imipenem nor ampicillin, suggesting that transfer of mycolates to arabinogalactan may require peptidoglycan precursor synthesis but not transpeptidation.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3B.

claim: Transfer of mycolates to arabinogalactan may require peptidoglycan precursor synthesis but not transpeptidation.
source: OalkTMM labeling was sensitive to d-cycloserine, but not to imipenem nor ampicillin, suggesting that transfer of mycolates to arabinogalactan may require peptidoglycan precursor synthesis but not transpeptidation.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential sensitivity of OalkTMM labeling to different antibiotics.

claim: Treatment with either d-cycloserine or imipenem resulted in dose-dependent inhibition of alkDA-derived fluorescence that plateaued at approximately half of untreated levels.
source: Treatment with either d-cycloserine or imipenem, but not ampicillin, resulted in dose-dependent inhibition of the probe-derived fluorescence that plateaued at approximately half of untreated levels.
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data in Figure 3C.

claim: Treatment with ampicillin did not result in dose-dependent inhibition of alkDA-derived fluorescence.
source: Treatment with either d-cycloserine or imipenem, but not ampicillin, resulted in dose-dependent inhibition of the probe-derived fluorescence that plateaued at approximately half of untreated levels.
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data in Figure 3C.

claim: The effects of d-cycloserine and imipenem on alkDA incorporation were the same or slightly greater than the potencies predicted by the antibiotics individually.
source: The effects of d-cycloserine and imipenem on alkDA incorporation were the same or slightly greater than the potencies predicted by the antibiotics individually (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by Bliss independence analysis in Figure 3D.

claim: The primarily additive nature of d-cycloserine and imipenem in the Bliss independence model is consistent with the idea that they block distinct pathways of alkDA incorporation.
source: The primarily additive nature of these antibiotics in the Bliss independence model is consistent with the idea that d-cycloserine and imipenem block distinct pathways of alkDA incorporation, and therefore that the probe incorporates into mycobacterial peptidoglycan via both cytoplasmic and l,d-transpeptidase routes.
evidence: This is inferred from the Bliss independence analysis results.

claim: alkDA incorporates into mycobacterial peptidoglycan via both cytoplasmic and l,d-transpeptidase routes.
source: The primarily additive nature of these antibiotics in the Bliss independence model is consistent with the idea that d-cycloserine and imipenem block distinct pathways of alkDA incorporation, and therefore that the probe incorporates into mycobacterial peptidoglycan via both cytoplasmic and l,d-transpeptidase routes.
evidence: This is inferred from the additive effects of d-cycloserine and imipenem on alkDA labeling.

claim: RADA and NADA labeling were more sensitive to imipenem than HADA and alkDA.
source: RADA and NADA labeling were more sensitive to imipenem than HADA and alkDA (Figure 3B), at multiple concentrations of drug (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by antibiotic sensitivity data in Figures 3B and 3E.

claim: M. tuberculosis homologs LdtMT1, LdtMT2, and LdtMT4 have been shown in vitro to have both cross-linking and d-amino acid exchange activity.
source: We chose to focus on LdtA, LdtB and LdtE because the M. tuberculosis homologs (LdtMT1, LdtMT2, and LdtMT4, respectively) have been shown in vitro to have both cross-linking and d-amino acid exchange activity and to be inhibited by imipenem (Cordillot et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to biochemical studies of M. tuberculosis l,d-transpeptidases.

claim: M. tuberculosis homologs LdtMT1, LdtMT2, and LdtMT4 are inhibited by imipenem.
source: We chose to focus on LdtA, LdtB and LdtE because the M. tuberculosis homologs (LdtMT1, LdtMT2, and LdtMT4, respectively) have been shown in vitro to have both cross-linking and d-amino acid exchange activity and to be inhibited by imipenem (Cordillot et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to biochemical studies of M. tuberculosis l,d-transpeptidases.

claim: RADA and NADA fluorescence decreased by ~80–85% in the absence of ldtABE.
source: RADA and NADA fluorescence decreased by ~80–85% the absence of ldtABE, and this effect was complemented by the expression of ldtA alone (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3F.

claim: The decrease in RADA and NADA fluorescence in the absence of ldtABE was complemented by the expression of ldtA alone.
source: RADA and NADA fluorescence decreased by ~80–85% the absence of ldtABE, and this effect was complemented by the expression of ldtA alone (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3F.

claim: HADA and alkDA labeling decreased by ~40–60% in the absence of ldtABE.
source: We observed a more moderate effect on HADA and alkDA labeling, which were decreased by ~40–60%.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3F.

claim: RADA and NADA probes primarily report l,d-transpeptidase activity, tetrapeptide substrate, or both.
source: Collectively these data suggest that: 1. RADA and NADA probes primarily report l,d-transpeptidase activity, tetrapeptide substrate, or both, and 2. HADA and alkDA likely label via both cytoplasmic and l,d-transpeptidase routes.
evidence: This is inferred from the high sensitivity of RADA and NADA to imipenem and ldtABE deletion.

claim: HADA and alkDA likely label via both cytoplasmic and l,d-transpeptidase routes.
source: Collectively these data suggest that: 1. RADA and NADA probes primarily report l,d-transpeptidase activity, tetrapeptide substrate, or both, and 2. HADA and alkDA likely label via both cytoplasmic and l,d-transpeptidase routes.
evidence: This is inferred from the partial sensitivity of HADA and alkDA to both d-cycloserine and imipenem.

claim: Peptidoglycan is remodeled at both the poles and along the sidewall in mycobacteria.
source: As RADA labeling in mycobacteria is largely indicative of l,d-transpeptidase activity (Figure 3) and occurs at the poles and along the sidewall (Figure 2), we surmise that peptidoglycan is remodeled at both of these locations.
evidence: This is inferred from the localization of RADA labeling and its dependence on l,d-transpeptidases.

claim: alkDADA labeling was relatively stable to imipenem treatment.
source: Consistent with this notion, and in contrast to the monopeptide probes, alkDADA labeling was relatively stable to imipenem treatment (Figure 3B and E) and inefficiently incorporated (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by antibiotic sensitivity data in Figures 3B and 3E.

claim: alkDADA was inefficiently incorporated.
source: Consistent with this notion, and in contrast to the monopeptide probes, alkDADA labeling was relatively stable to imipenem treatment (Figure 3B and E) and inefficiently incorporated (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 showing lower fluorescence intensity for alkDADA compared to alkDA at similar concentrations.

claim: Overall labeling by alkDADA decreased in the absence of LdtA, LdtB, LdtE or combinations thereof.
source: Thus we were surprised to observe that overall labeling by alkDADA decreased in the absence of LdtA, LdtB, LdtE or combinations thereof (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The reduction in alkDADA signal in ldt mutants occurred primarily at the poles.
source: The reduction in signal occurred primarily at the poles (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B) yet loss of the enzymes did not impair bacterial growth (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Loss of LdtA, LdtB, and LdtE did not impair bacterial growth.
source: The reduction in signal occurred primarily at the poles (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B) yet loss of the enzymes did not impair bacterial growth (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by growth curve data in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: d-alanine is produced in mycobacteria by Alr, the d-alanine racemase.
source: d-alanine is produced in mycobacteria by Alr, the d-alanine racemase (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is established knowledge about d-alanine biosynthesis.

claim: d-alanine is linked to a second d-alanine by DdlA, the d-alanine ligase.
source: The molecule is linked to a second d-alanine by DdlA, the d-alanine ligase, and the resulting dipeptide is added to the UDP-MurNAc-tripeptide by MurF.
evidence: This is established knowledge about peptidoglycan precursor biosynthesis.

claim: The d-alanine-d-alanine dipeptide is added to the UDP-MurNAc-tripeptide by MurF.
source: The molecule is linked to a second d-alanine by DdlA, the d-alanine ligase, and the resulting dipeptide is added to the UDP-MurNAc-tripeptide by MurF.
evidence: This is established knowledge about peptidoglycan precursor biosynthesis.

claim: Growth of Δalr is rescued by exogenous d-alanine.
source: We first constructed an alr deletion mutant in M. smegmatis and verified that growth is rescued by exogenous d-alanine but not by alkDA (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by growth rescue data in Figure 4A.

claim: Growth of Δalr is not rescued by alkDA.
source: We first constructed an alr deletion mutant in M. smegmatis and verified that growth is rescued by exogenous d-alanine but not by alkDA (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by growth rescue data in Figure 4A.

claim: Δalr growth was rescued by d-alanine-d-alanine.
source: In contrast to the alkDA results, we were able to rescue alr with either d-alanine-d-alanine or its alkynyl derivative (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by growth rescue data in Figure 4A.

claim: Δalr growth was rescued by alkDADA.
source: In contrast to the alkDA results, we were able to rescue alr with either d-alanine-d-alanine or its alkynyl derivative (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by growth rescue data in Figure 4A.

claim: alkDADA rescues the growth of a temperature-sensitive ddlA mutant at the non-permissive temperature.
source: Therefore, we confirmed that alkDADA rescues the growth of a temperature-sensitive ddlA mutant (Belanger et al., 2000) at the non-permissive temperature (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by growth rescue data in Figure 4B.

claim: A low-molecular-weight band that is reduced upon d-cycloserine treatment and accumulates when MurJ is depleted or vancomycin is added was detected from M. smegmatis extracts.
source: We detected a biotin-linked, low-molecular-weight band that is reduced upon d-cycloserine treatment and accumulates when the lipid II flippase MurJ (MviN, (Gee et al., 2012)) is depleted or vancomycin is added (Figure 5A), conditions that have been shown to dramatically enhance precursor detection in other species (Qiao et al., 2014; Qiao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 5A.

claim: The BDL-marked species detected from M. smegmatis extracts are lipid-linked peptidoglycan precursors.
source: These data strongly suggest that the BDL-marked species are lipid-linked peptidoglycan precursors.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavior of the detected band under conditions known to affect precursor levels.

claim: A low molecular-weight species that accumulated with vancomycin treatment was detected from Δalr incubated with alkDADA.
source: Accordingly, we repeated the experiment in the Δalr background and found that we could clearly detect a low molecular-weight species band that accumulated with vancomycin treatment (Figure 5B, top) and that ran at the same size as BDL-labeled material (Figure 5B, bottom).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 5B.

claim: The alkDADA-labeled species detected from Δalr ran at the same size as BDL-labeled material.
source: Accordingly, we repeated the experiment in the Δalr background and found that we could clearly detect a low molecular-weight species band that accumulated with vancomycin treatment (Figure 5B, top) and that ran at the same size as BDL-labeled material (Figure 5B, bottom).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 5B.

claim: A low-molecular-weight species was detected from Δalr incubated with azDADA that was revealed by CuAAC ligation to alkyne-biotin.
source: We were also able to identify a low-molecular-weight species from Δalr incubated with azDADA that was revealed by either CuAAC or SPAAC ligation to alkyne- or cyclooctyne-biotin, respectively (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 5C.

claim: A low-molecular-weight species was detected from Δalr incubated with azDADA that was revealed by SPAAC ligation to cyclooctyne-biotin.
source: We were also able to identify a low-molecular-weight species from Δalr incubated with azDADA that was revealed by either CuAAC or SPAAC ligation to alkyne- or cyclooctyne-biotin, respectively (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 5C.

claim: The alkDADA and azDADA probes insert into mycobacterial peptidoglycan precursors by a MurF-dependent route.
source: Taken together, our genetic and biochemical experiments show that the alkDADA and azDADA probes insert into mycobacterial peptidoglycan precursors by a MurF-dependent route.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of genetic rescue experiments and biochemical detection of labeled precursors.

claim: The final, lipid-linked peptidoglycan precursor lipid II is synthesized by MurG on the cytoplasmic side of the plasma membrane.
source: The final, lipid-linked peptidoglycan precursor lipid II is synthesized by MurG on the cytoplasmic side of the plasma membrane then flipped to the periplasm and polymerized [Figure 3—figure supplement 1, (Zhao et al., 2017)].
evidence: This is established knowledge about lipid II biosynthesis, supported by citation.

claim: Lipid II is flipped to the periplasm and polymerized.
source: The final, lipid-linked peptidoglycan precursor lipid II is synthesized by MurG on the cytoplasmic side of the plasma membrane then flipped to the periplasm and polymerized [Figure 3—figure supplement 1, (Zhao et al., 2017)].
evidence: This is established knowledge about lipid II processing, supported by citation.

claim: MurG fused to two different fluorescent proteins and expressed under two different promoters is present at both the poles and periphery of M. smegmatis.
source: We previously showed that MurG fused to two different fluorescent proteins and expressed under two different promoters is present at both the poles and periphery of M. smegmatis (Meniche et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Labeling by alkDADA marks similar subcellular locations as MurG even with pulses as short as ~1% generation time.
source: Labeling by alkDADA marks similar subcellular locations even with pulses as short as ~1% generation time (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Lipid-linked peptidoglycan precursors are synthesized at lateral sites in addition to their expected localization at the poles.
source: These data suggest that lipid-linked peptidoglycan precursors are synthesized at lateral sites in addition to their expected localization at the poles.
evidence: This is inferred from the localization of alkDADA labeling and MurG.

claim: Fluorescent vancomycin binds uncrosslinked peptidoglycan pentapeptides and does not normally cross the plasma membrane.
source: This reagent binds uncrosslinked peptidoglycan pentapeptides and does not normally cross the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is established knowledge about fluorescent vancomycin properties.

claim: Pentapeptide monomers are a low abundant species in M. tuberculosis, M. abscessus and M. leprae peptidoglycan.
source: Pentapeptide monomers are a low abundant species in M. tuberculosis, M. abscessus and M. leprae peptidoglycan (Kumar et al., 2012; Mahapatra et al., 2008; Lavollay et al., 2008; Lavollay et al., 2011), suggesting that fluorescent vancomycin primarily reports extracellular, lipid-linked precursors in this genus.
evidence: This is supported by citations to peptidoglycan composition studies.

claim: Fluorescent vancomycin primarily reports extracellular, lipid-linked precursors in mycobacteria.
source: Pentapeptide monomers are a low abundant species in M. tuberculosis, M. abscessus and M. leprae peptidoglycan (Kumar et al., 2012; Mahapatra et al., 2008; Lavollay et al., 2008; Lavollay et al., 2011), suggesting that fluorescent vancomycin primarily reports extracellular, lipid-linked precursors in this genus.
evidence: This is inferred from the low abundance of pentapeptides in mature peptidoglycan.

claim: Labeling of M. smegmatis with fluorescent vancomycin revealed both polar and lateral patches.
source: Labeling of M. smegmatis with this probe revealed both polar and lateral patches (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) as previously noted (Singh et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: At least some of the peptidoglycan precursors present along the periphery of the mycobacterial cell are flipped to the periplasm.
source: This observation suggests that at least some of the peptidoglycan precursors present along the periphery of the mycobacterial cell are flipped to the periplasm.
evidence: This is inferred from the fluorescent vancomycin labeling pattern.

claim: Transglycosylases from both the PBP and SEDS families stitch peptidoglycan precursors into the existing meshwork.
source: Transglycosylases from both the PBP (penicillin-binding proteins) and SEDS (shape, elongation, division, and sporulation) families stitch peptidoglycan precursors into the existing meshwork (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, [Boutte et al., 2016; Hayashi et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2017; Cho et al., 2016; Meeske et al., 2016; Leclercq et al., 2017; Arora et al., 2018]).
evidence: This is established knowledge about peptidoglycan polymerization, supported by multiple citations.

claim: PonA1 and PonA2 are two conserved PBPs in mycobacteria that are likely responsible for most of the peptidoglycan polymerization required for cell viability.
source: Two conserved PBPs in mycobacteria are likely responsible for most of the peptidoglycan polymerization required for cell viability, PonA1 and PonA2 (7, 19, 59).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on mycobacterial PBPs.

claim: A subset of PonA1-mRFP homes to the lateral cell surface.
source: We found that a subset of this fusion protein indeed homes to the lateral cell surface (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Fluorescent derivatives of β-lactam antibiotics bind specifically and covalently to PBPs.
source: Fluorescent derivatives of β-lactam antibiotics bind specifically and covalently to PBPs, and therefore have been used to image active enzyme in both protein gels and intact cells (Kocaoglu and Carlson, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about fluorescent β-lactam probes, supported by citation.

claim: Bocillin binds both the poles and sidewall of M. smegmatis.
source: Our images of whole cells labeled with Bocillin, a BODIPY conjugate of penicillin, were in agreement with those from a previous publication (Plocinski et al., 2011), and seemed to indicate that Bocillin binds both the poles and sidewall of M. smegmatis (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B and C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data in Figure 5—figure supplement 3B and C.

claim: Fluorescence across the cell surface from Bocillin was diminished by pre-treating cells with ampicillin.
source: Fluorescence across the cell surface was diminished by pre-treating cells with the β-lactam ampicillin, which prevents peptidoglycan assembly by binding to PBPs, but not d-cycloserine, which inhibits peptidoglycan synthesis in a PBP-independent manner (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B and C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data in Figure 5—figure supplement 3B and C.

claim: Fluorescence across the cell surface from Bocillin was not diminished by pre-treating cells with d-cycloserine.
source: Fluorescence across the cell surface was diminished by pre-treating cells with the β-lactam ampicillin, which prevents peptidoglycan assembly by binding to PBPs, but not d-cycloserine, which inhibits peptidoglycan synthesis in a PBP-independent manner (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B and C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data in Figure 5—figure supplement 3B and C.

claim: At least some of the sidewall labeling of Bocillin is specific.
source: These experiments suggest that at least some of the sidewall labeling of Bocillin is specific, and therefore, that PBPs are present and active in these locations.
evidence: This is inferred from the ampicillin-sensitivity of Bocillin labeling.

claim: PBPs are present and active along the sidewall of M. smegmatis.
source: These experiments suggest that at least some of the sidewall labeling of Bocillin is specific, and therefore, that PBPs are present and active in these locations.
evidence: This is inferred from the specific Bocillin labeling at the sidewall.

claim: Peptidoglycan precursors are made and likely polymerized both at the poles and sidewall.
source: Our data indicate that peptidoglycan precursors are made and likely polymerized both at the poles and sidewall.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of dipeptide labeling, fluorescent vancomycin staining, and PBP localization data.

claim: Dispersed elongation has not been reported in mycobacteria.
source: However, dispersed elongation has not been reported in mycobacteria.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Fluorescence dilution in the pulse-chase experiment was consistent with previous reports and restricted to the mycobacterial poles.
source: While we cannot rule out sidewall expansion below our limit of detection, the fluorescence dilution in this experiment was consistent with previous reports (Aldridge et al., 2012; Santi et al., 2013; Meniche et al., 2014; Kieser and Rubin, 2014; Boutte et al., 2016; Rego et al., 2017) and restricted to the mycobacterial poles (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by pulse-chase microscopy data in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: Extended incubation of M. smegmatis (~48 hr) with lysozyme substantially decreases colony-forming units.
source: Extended incubation of M. smegmatis (~48 hr) with the peptidoglycan-degrading enzyme lysozyme substantially decreases colony-forming units (Kanetsuna, 1980).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on lysozyme effects on M. smegmatis.

claim: Spheroplasts generated by combined glycine and lysozyme treatment lack peptidoglycan.
source: We have also shown that spheroplasts generated by combined glycine and lysozyme treatment lack peptidoglycan (Melzer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study by the authors.

claim: Lysozyme is able to access and damage peptidoglycan in intact M. smegmatis cells.
source: Together these data indicate that the enzyme is able to access and damage peptidoglycan in intact cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the effects of lysozyme on colony-forming units and spheroplast formation.

claim: Pre-treatment by muramidases shifted alkDADA fluorescence from the brighter pole towards the sidewall.
source: Pre-treatment by the muramidases clearly shifted the fluorescence from the brighter pole towards the sidewall (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data in Figure 6B.

claim: Mycobacteria reallocate peptidoglycan assembly away from the faster growing pole and toward the periphery upon damage to the cell wall.
source: These data indicate that mycobacteria reallocate peptidoglycan assembly away from the faster growing pole and toward the periphery upon damage to the cell wall (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is inferred from the shift in alkDADA labeling after muramidase treatment.

claim: In M. smegmatis the metabolic fate of monopeptide probes is partially dependent on the substituent.
source: Here, we show that in M. smegmatis the metabolic fate of monopeptide probes is partially dependent on the substituent; whereas NBD and TAMRA-conjugated d-amino acids are primarily exchanged into mycobacterial peptidoglycan by l,d-transpeptidases, their alkyne and coumarin-conjugated counterparts appear to incorporate by both extracellular and intracellular pathways (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by antibiotic sensitivity and mutant analysis data.

claim: NBD and TAMRA-conjugated d-amino acids are primarily exchanged into mycobacterial peptidoglycan by l,d-transpeptidases.
source: Here, we show that in M. smegmatis the metabolic fate of monopeptide probes is partially dependent on the substituent; whereas NBD and TAMRA-conjugated d-amino acids are primarily exchanged into mycobacterial peptidoglycan by l,d-transpeptidases, their alkyne and coumarin-conjugated counterparts appear to incorporate by both extracellular and intracellular pathways (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by antibiotic sensitivity and mutant analysis data.

claim: Alkyne and coumarin-conjugated d-amino acids appear to incorporate by both extracellular and intracellular pathways.
source: Here, we show that in M. smegmatis the metabolic fate of monopeptide probes is partially dependent on the substituent; whereas NBD and TAMRA-conjugated d-amino acids are primarily exchanged into mycobacterial peptidoglycan by l,d-transpeptidases, their alkyne and coumarin-conjugated counterparts appear to incorporate by both extracellular and intracellular pathways (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by antibiotic sensitivity and mutant analysis data.

claim: This is the first direct demonstration that peptidoglycan precursors can be metabolically labeled in vivo without radioactivity.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first direct demonstration that peptidoglycan precursors can be metabolically labeled in vivo without radioactivity.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study's findings.

claim: The lateral surface of mycobacteria does not appear to contribute to cell elongation under normal growth conditions.
source: The lateral surface of mycobacteria does not appear to contribute to cell elongation under normal growth conditions (Figure 5—figure supplement 4, [Aldridge et al., 2012; Santi et al., 2013; Meniche et al., 2014; Kieser and Rubin, 2014; Boutte et al., 2016]) but nevertheless hosts a substantial portion of envelope synthesis and remodeling.
evidence: This is supported by pulse-chase data and citations to previous studies.

claim: The lateral surface of mycobacteria hosts a substantial portion of envelope synthesis and remodeling.
source: The lateral surface of mycobacteria does not appear to contribute to cell elongation under normal growth conditions (Figure 5—figure supplement 4, [Aldridge et al., 2012; Santi et al., 2013; Meniche et al., 2014; Kieser and Rubin, 2014; Boutte et al., 2016]) but nevertheless hosts a substantial portion of envelope synthesis and remodeling.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by probe labeling data.

claim: The twofold ratio of fast/bright:slow/dim pole fluorescence roughly corresponds to previous estimates of intracellular differences in polar elongation.
source: The twofold ratio of fast/bright:slow/dim pole fluorescence (Figures 2C, D and 6B) roughly corresponds to previous estimates of intracellular differences in polar elongation (Aldridge et al., 2012; Joyce et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of fluorescence ratios and citations to previous studies.

claim: Diminished polarity and asymmetry is apparent in the sub-population of M. tuberculosis that is labeled by alkDADA and OalkTMM.
source: Diminished polarity and asymmetry is also apparent in the sub-population of M. tuberculosis that is labeled by alkDADA and OalkTMM (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The data are in agreement with the heterogeneity in polar dominance observed previously for M. tuberculosis.
source: Our data are in agreement with the heterogeneity in polar dominance observed previously for M. tuberculosis (Botella et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study on M. tuberculosis growth patterns.

claim: Sidewall envelope metabolism may be even more prominent in M. tuberculosis than in M. smegmatis, comprising 70–75% of the total cell output.
source: Although we cannot rule out a contribution from cyan autofluorescence, these experiments also suggest that sidewall envelope metabolism may be even more prominent in M. tuberculosis than in M. smegmatis, comprising 70–75% of the total cell output.
evidence: This is inferred from the quantitative comparison of sidewall labeling between the two species.

claim: It is possible that peptidoglycan assembly along the lateral surface of the mycobacterial cell is simply a byproduct of synthetic enzymes that are en route to the polar elongasome or the divisome.
source: It is possible that peptidoglycan assembly along the lateral surface of the mycobacterial cell is simply a byproduct of synthetic enzymes that are en route to the polar elongasome or the divisome.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative explanation for sidewall peptidoglycan synthesis.

claim: Having active enzymes at the ready could enable efficient coordination between cell growth and septation.
source: Having active enzymes at the ready could enable efficient coordination between cell growth and septation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential benefits of having enzymes distributed along the cell.

claim: Cell wall synthesis along the periphery could allow mycobacteria to edit what would otherwise be an inert surface.
source: Instead we propose that cell wall synthesis along the periphery could allow mycobacteria to edit what would otherwise be an inert surface (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the function of sidewall peptidoglycan synthesis.

claim: Peptidoglycan and mycomembrane metabolism along the periphery may thicken or fill in the gaps of envelope that was initially deposited at the poles or the septum.
source: Peptidoglycan and mycomembrane metabolism in this region may thicken or fill in the gaps of envelope that was initially deposited at the poles or the septum and enable the bacterium to correct stochastic defects and repair damage.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential functions of sidewall metabolism.

claim: Sidewall metabolism may enable the bacterium to correct stochastic defects and repair damage.
source: Peptidoglycan and mycomembrane metabolism in this region may thicken or fill in the gaps of envelope that was initially deposited at the poles or the septum and enable the bacterium to correct stochastic defects and repair damage.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential functions of sidewall metabolism, supported by the damage response data.

claim: The ability to tailor the entire cell surface should enable rapid adaptation to external stimuli.
source: More broadly, the ability to tailor the entire cell surface, not just the ends, should enable rapid adaptation to external stimuli.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential advantages of sidewall metabolism.

claim: The ability to tailor the entire cell surface may be particularly important for M. tuberculosis, a slow-growing organism that must survive a hostile, nutrient-poor environment.
source: Such activity may be particularly important for M. tuberculosis, a slow-growing organism that must survive a hostile, nutrient-poor environment.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential importance of sidewall metabolism for M. tuberculosis.
